title: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events
description: Compare WebSockets and Server-Sent Events to understand when each real-time communication pattern is appropriate.

data.text: Standard HTTP is request-response: the client asks, the server answers. Real-time applications need something different. **WebSockets** and **Server-Sent Events** are the two main browser-native options for pushing data from server to client. They solve similar problems with very different architectures.

WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent, bidirectional TCP channel. After the handshake, both client and server can send messages at any time. This makes WebSockets ideal for interactive applications like chat, gaming, or collaborative editing.

items: Full-duplex: both sides send data independently
Starts as HTTP, then upgrades via 101 Switching Protocols
Requires custom framing and heartbeat mechanisms
More complex server infrastructure

data.text: Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a much simpler pattern: a single, long-lived HTTP connection where only the server sends text-based events. The browser receives them through a simple EventSource API.

items: Unidirectional: server to client only
Built on standard HTTP; works with standard servers and proxies
Automatic reconnection by the browser
Text-based event format, ideal for notifications and feeds

cards.title: WebSockets
items: Client and server both send messages
Custom protocol over TCP
Better for chat, gaming, co-editing
More complex scaling and load balancing

cards.title: Server-Sent Events
items: Server pushes events to client
Standard HTTP GET with streaming
Great for live updates and notifications
Works easily through proxies and CDNs

data.caption: Communication direction for WebSockets and Server-Sent Events
data.mermaid:
graph TD
    C[Client] <-->|bidirectional| W[WebSockets]
    C -->|receive only| S[Server-Sent Events]
    S -.->|server pushes events| C

data.title: Start with SSE when possible
data.text: If your application only needs server-to-client updates, SSE is simpler to implement, debug, and scale. Move to WebSockets only when you genuinely need client-to-server streaming.

items: WebSockets require sticky sessions or a shared message bus to scale across servers.
SSE works with standard HTTP load balancers because it uses ordinary HTTP connections.
Both patterns consume server resources per connection; plan capacity accordingly.
Serverless environments may have connection duration limits that affect long-lived streams.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: WebSockets provide true bidirectional communication over a persistent TCP channel.
SSE provides simple server-to-client streaming over standard HTTP.
SSE is easier to deploy and scale for one-way updates.
Choose the simpler pattern that satisfies your actual communication needs.
data.takeaway: Real-time communication is not one-size-fits-all. Match the protocol to the direction and complexity of your data flow.

items.question: Can I use both in the same application?
items.answer: Yes. Many applications use WebSockets for chat or collaboration and SSE for live status updates or notifications.

items.question: Does SSE work with HTTP/2?
items.answer: Yes. SSE is just an HTTP response with a special content type. It works with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. HTTP/3 support is also growing.

items.question: What happens if a WebSocket connection drops?
items.answer: The client must detect the disconnection and reconnect, usually with exponential backoff. Libraries like Socket.IO handle reconnection automatically.

data.text: The best real-time protocol is the simplest one that solves your specific communication problem.
